analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent federal board to investigate police killings, shootings, and severe-injury cases.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in two House committees since its introduction on May 29, 2025, with six House sponsors total, all Democrats, and no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new, independent federal agency — a National Police Misuse of Force Investigation Board — to investigate every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe injury. It would work much like the National Transportation Safety Board does for plane crashes: gathering facts, releasing public reports, and issuing recommendations that agencies must answer in writing. States and cities that accept certain federal policing grants would have to make the Board's findings usable in court and file yearly progress reports, or risk losing up to 10 percent of those grant funds. The Board itself could not fire officers or bring charges; its enforcement power comes through public reports and the Justice Department's authority to pursue police departments showing patterns of abuse.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of people killed or seriously injured by police, who would get a designated federal family-support contact, funded counseling through an independent nonprofit, briefings before any public statement, and access to an independent investigation instead of relying only on the local department investigating its own officers. Communities affected by police violence would gain public reports with demographic data on victims and officers, and federal officials would gain subpoena power to compel testimony and records that local investigations often cannot reach.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people killed or injured by police

how_it_helps.text: The Board would be required to investigate and establish the facts of every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe bodily injury in custody [S2].
Investigations would cover demographic data on the person killed or injured and the officers involved, the reason for the initial contact, the events leading up to the force, and the outcome [S2].

As soon as practicable after a fatal or serious-injury incident, the Board would designate a family-support director and an independent nonprofit to provide mental health and counseling services, and families would be briefed before any public briefing on the investigation [S2].

The Board could hold hearings, issue subpoenas enforceable in federal court, enter and inspect scenes, preserve and test involved weapons, and order autopsies — powers local investigators often lack or decline to use against a colleague's department [S2].

Investigation records would generally be made available to the public on request, and recipients of Board recommendations must formally respond in writing within 90 days, with responses made public [S2].

States and localities receiving certain federal policing grants would have to make Board findings admissible in criminal and civil court and submit yearly reports on their progress implementing recommendations, or face a reduction of 1 to 10 percent of those funds at the Attorney General's discretion [S2].
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division could open pattern-or-practice investigations of departments citing lack of progress on Board recommendations and take direct enforcement action [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new agency, with an open-ended appropriation, staff in every state more than 1,000 miles from a regional office, and annual audits by the Comptroller General. Police departments and state and local governments would bear the compliance burden: mandatory reports to the Board and Congress, written responses to every recommendation, and potential cuts of 1 to 10 percent of Byrne/JAG grant funds if they do not comply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, police departments, and state grant recipients

drawbacks.text: The Board would be recommendatory, not a prosecutor: it could not discipline officers, bring charges, or force any department to change, so accountability would still depend on local prosecutors, the Justice Department, and agencies choosing to act [S2].

Section 15, adapted from aviation law, would generally bar parties in a civil lawsuit from obtaining body-camera or vehicle-mounted footage through discovery except by court order for a fair trial, and would prohibit using Board reports in civil damages actions — provisions that could limit the very families the bill aims to help in their own lawsuits [S2].

Parts of the text appear copied from the National Transportation Safety Board statute, including a qualification barring public inquiry members with a 'pecuniary interest in an aviation enterprise' and leftover provisions about hazardous-materials transport, which raises questions about the drafting's fit for policing [S2].
There is no funding level: the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary,' leaving the cost of a new agency with at least one full-time investigator in many states entirely open-ended [S2].

The Board would overlap with existing investigations by the Justice Department, state bureaus, and local prosecutors, potentially duplicating work or creating conflicts over which agency controls a scene and evidence [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families who today watch a local department investigate its own officers, an independent federal investigation with subpoena power, public reports, and paid family support is a real, concrete gain. But the design has rough edges: the Board's only hard tools are public reports and, indirectly, grant penalties and Justice Department pattern-or-practice suits; the civil-litigation restrictions on body-camera footage cut against victims' own lawsuits; and the open-ended cost of a nationwide investigative agency is unpriced. The bill's fate, however, makes the weighing largely hypothetical — it has attracted six supporters in the House and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, where no hearing, markup, or floor action has been scheduled so far this Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) introduced H.R. 3652 on May 29, 2025, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-MS), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-DC), and Jim McGovern (D-MA) [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction [S4].
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The action history shows no activity beyond introduction and committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost anything material yet, since the bill has not moved: police departments and their associations are spared new federal investigation and grant conditions for now, while families of people killed or injured by police have gained no new avenue of independent investigation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police departments spared new federal oversight, for now

against.name: Police unions and state and local law enforcement agencies
against.role: Organized opposition to federal police-accountability mechanisms
against.what_they_did: These groups have consistently opposed independent federal investigation of officer use of force, and the bill would subject their members and departments to subpoena-backed federal investigations, mandatory reporting, and grant penalties.

sides.party_line_note: All six House sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; there has been no vote, so no roll-call split exists, but the sponsorship pattern is entirely one-sided.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would subject departments to subpoena-backed federal investigations of every custody death, shooting, and severe-injury case, require public written responses to recommendations, and expose noncompliant grant recipients to cuts of 1–10 percent of Byrne/JAG funds. Departments would lose the current arrangement in which local agencies largely investigate their own officers.

Independent federal investigations with public demographic reporting would replace the internal-process control unions currently have over discipline records and use-of-force reviews in most jurisdictions. Officer groups have historically opposed such outside review.

industries.industry: Nonprofit victim-support and mental health organizations
industries.note: The bill would require the Board to designate an independent nonprofit with primary responsibility for counseling and support to affected families after every fatal or serious-injury incident, creating a funded, defined role for such organizations.

The Board could recommend 'manufacturing or acquisition changes related to the weapons and equipment issued to the police force,' which could expose products to scrutiny, though only as nonbinding recommendations.

analysis.trajectory: With six supporters in a 435-member House, no action from either committee of jurisdiction since the May 2025 referral, and Republican control of both committees, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or floor vote this Congress. Bills of this type have historically needed much broader sponsorship and a committee champion to advance; nothing in the record suggests that is forming.
